PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:24 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11413-5 Advances in machine learning for wetland classification: a comprehensive survey of methods and applications Derrick Effah1 · Ali Zia2,3 · Mohammad Awrangjeb1 · Yongsheng Gao4 · Kwabena Sarpong1 Received: 15 March 2025 / Accepted: 30 September 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Wetlands are critical ecosystems supporting biodiversity and providing essential environ- mental services. With increasing threats to wetlands, efficient classification techniques are essential for effective conservation. Several researchers have contributed to wetland clas- sification across reputable journals. However, some challenges (data scarcity, noisy labels, and model generalisability) still exist. Therefore, this paper presents a comprehensive sur- vey of recent advancements in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) for wetland classification, focusing on developments from 2018 to 2025. Key methodologies, includ- ing convolutional neural networks, transformers, and generative adversarial networks, are critically reviewed, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and applications in remote sensing. Unlike previous reviews, this work emphasises underexplored techniques such as few-shot learning and Mamba networks, offering practical recommendations for handling limited training data and improving model generalisability. The study also identifies prom- ising research directions, such as test-time training and hybrid loss functions, to address challenges in wetland classification. This survey aims to guide researchers and practitio- ners in advancing state-of-the-art wetland classification through ML and DL technologies. Keywords Deep learning · Machine learning · Survey · Wetland classification 1 Introduction Wetlands encompass tracts of land either submerged in water or thoroughly soaked with water. Usually, the water permeates and accumulates from an underground aquifer or spring. These can also be formed by lakes, rivers or seas, particularly in coastal zones. Coastal wetlands are crucial and valuable ecosystems that are strongly linked to human well-being. They play a vital role in preserving biodiversity, purifying water, protecting against storm surges, sequestering carbon, regulating microclimates, and more Mitsch et al. (2013). How- ever, there has been significant degradation of wetlands over the years, which is detrimental to global and regional biodiversity (Gardner and Finlayson 2018). For this reason, it is dire to map wetlands on regional and global scales for strategic conservation purposes. GIS gives the tools and systems for analysing and visualising spatial data (Rychlicki et al. 2020). GPS provides precise geospatial coordinates of objects on the field that can be used for georeferencing and ground truth data to verify satellite and airborne data. These technolo- gies make a robust framework that underpins wetland classification. Also, the availability of RS data necessitates big data analytics in the geographic information space, paving the way for combined RS, ML and DL as advanced analytical approaches. Due to advancements in passive and active RS, space-based sensors are becoming more precise and valuable in determining the characteristics of wetlands and distinguishing different types of land use and land cover (Jafarzadeh et al. 2022). Moreover, aerial RS with high spatial resolution is significant in characterising the ground features. High spatial and spectral resolution data offer a wealth of information for wetland assessment. Consequently, fine-grained classification of wetlands using RS data has become a prominent research space (Dronova et al. 2021). Despite the considerable advancement in technologies, RS-based wetland classification proves to be a challenging endeavour (Tiner et al. 2015). These maps have generally included wetlands as a category that gives insight into the extent of wetlands across the globe (Zomer et al. 2009; Jafarzadeh et al. 2022). Depending on the task, researchers have focused on static mapping and multi-temporal mapping. For instance, Huang et al. (2023) focused on designing an adver- sarial network algorithm to handle cross-scene classification rather than the mapping objec- tive. We have discussed the temporal dimensions in the following sections. 3.2.1 Static mapping The aim of static wetland mapping is to capture the spatial extent of the characteristics of wetlands at a single point in time by using a single date of imagery. Static mapping is very simple and mainly used for quick decision-making. The 2D CNN and U-Net are mainly used for such static mapping because they have no internal gate to carry information for- ward in time. However, they are optimised for 2D spatial segmentation. For example, the skip connections in U-Net were built for accurate pixel segmentation, which is good for delineating wetland boundaries on one image. Therefore, we recommend that researchers and RS professionals who intend to map stable wetlands or create a baseline survey use U-Net or 2D CNNS. A classical example from the literature was proposed by (Peña et al. 2024). Peña et al. (2024) proposed a DeepAqua model based on the U-Net architecture to delineate water in a wetland area from a Sentinel 1 and 2 datasets with impressive perfor- mance over traditional ML algorithms. Moreover, Martins et al. (2020) proposed a deep neural network for complex wetland mapping using WorldView-3 and airborne LiDAR data with good performance. Again, Yang et al. (2022) used only the Sentinel-2 MSI for wetlands classification using CNN models. They found that the DensNet121 model outperformed others in overall accuracy and Kappa coefficient. Mahdianpari et al. (2018) utilised a deep CNN for complex wetland mapping. The authors fine-tuned a pretrained DL model, such as AlexNet, and compared the results with RF. Evidently, the CNN outperformed the RF, which signifies that neural networks will outperform traditional ML from the simplest to the most complex tasks. 3.2.2 Multi-temporal mapping Multi-temporal mapping utilises data from multiple time points, mainly to understand the temporal dynamics of wetlands over time. In doing so, it involves analysing a time series of satellite data or repeated ground surveys. Multi-temporal analysis gives more standardi- sation to areas that are truly wetlands or wetland-like vegetation temporarily. Here, recur- rent neural networks such as Long and Short Term Memory Networks can be employed for improved classification. Multi-temporal mapping requires sensors with a regular revisit time. Here, we recommend that researchers use Sentinel 1 and 2 datasets for their multi- temporal analysis. Sentinel 2 has a regular revisit time of 5 days at the equator, making it plausible to track seasonal vegetation dynamics and flooding cycles. Moreover, Sentinel 1 provides SAR data that has the ability to penetrate clouds and smoke, which can be used for all-weather vegetation mapping. However, researchers have focused on fusion strategies at different levels (pixel-level, feature-level or decision-level). In Fig. 5, we provide data fusion strategies and their key techniques that could be applied by researchers and professionals. The majority of wetlands studies used the feature-level fusion strategy, which offers good control over dimensionality with better feature alignment. Based on these characteristics, we recommend feature-level fusion that offers accuracy gains without increasing computa- tional overheads. These include atmospheric correc- tions, cloud masking, noise reduction and geometric correction. Atmospheric correction is done to eliminate the effect of atmospheric gases, aerosols and water vapour to retrieve surface reflectance (Vanhellemont and Ruddick 2018). Algorithms such as Sen2Cor are mostly used for atmospheric correction of Sentinel products. Salt-and- pepper noise can be removed by spatial filtering; in some cases, the wavelet transform can be used to decompose the signal into multiple frequency bands for noise filtering. Also, DL techniques can be used to denoise imagery, especially hyperspectral and SAR data. Aside from the use of spectral thresholding for cloud masking, DL techniques can be used for pixel-wise cloud detection. In geometric correction, raw images are aligned with real- world coordinates to account for distortions caused by sensor motion before further analy- sis. In addition, transformer-based models are able to outperform CNN models due to their ability to model long-distance feature channels in HSI, inherent in their long-range dependency capability, making them useful for hyperspectral wetland image classification. However, they require substantial computational resources that might not be efficient in resource-constrained envi- ronmental monitoring tools and devices. The use of unsupervised techniques, such as domain generalisation networks, is useful for cross-domain and cross-scene classification, which contributes to reducing spectral vari- ability across scenes. However, they require extensive training on source datasets, which are not readily available. To this end, researchers have developed models based on U-Net architecture (Peña et al. 2024), transformer architecture (Ke et al. 2024), and datasets such as HSI only, HSI and MSI (Gao et al. 2021), HSI and LiDAR (Guo et al. 2024) and MSI and SAR (Peña et al. 2024). Going forward, unsupervised and self-supervised learning will be useful for HSI wet- land image classification. For example, the high dimensionality of HSI can be reduced by unsupervised techniques such as principal components analysis (PCA), autoencoders, or independent component analysis. These algorithms can be leveraged to reduce the dimen- sionality of HSI data while retaining relevant features for downstream tasks. Again, unsu- pervised techniques can be used to solve the limited labelled data problem. Unsupervised techniques can be harnessed to group pixels of similar spectral and spatial characteristics into clusters, serving as a precursor for supervised or weakly supervised models. However, noisy data threatens the correctness of dimensionality reduction algorithms. For instance, techniques such as PCA for dimensionality reduction may capture noise as a significant component, leading to poor feature representation. Even so, this problem can be mitigated using regularisation techniques such as MixUp, which can be used to prevent the model from overfitting to noise. This must be a careful architectural design to optimally incorporate the strength of individual models into one. Some researchers hybridised GANs with transformer models to solve the limited labelled problem, but these transformer mod- els are downsized by their quadratic computational complexity. However, redundant layers can be pruned to offset the computational complexity. In the advent of imbalanced classes, focal loss or a variant of it should be used to improve model performance. Wetland data are prone to data imbalance problems, and as such, focal loss should be considered when defin- ing the optimisation function. In addition, innovative architectures such as Mamba can be employed to alleviate the complexity of transformer computations. Also, weakly supervised techniques such as few-shot learning can be utilised to handle limited training samples and noisy labels. Secondly, domain generalisation: Wetland dynamics present spectral shifts due to sea- sonal phenological variation, adding to the complexity of wetland areas. Researchers have been using domain adaptation and generalisation networks to solve cross-domain generali- sation. However, these networks require extensive source data to achieve a better perfor- mance in the testing phase without re-training. Fortunately, test-time training, as discussed in this review, offers a compelling alternative to domain generalisation networks in cross- domain generalisation, which alleviates the extensive source data requirement. However, future research should look into how TTT can be employed on HSI data since it was origi- nally designed for RGB data. Thirdly, data source: The Majority of the wetland studies utilised satellite data since they are free and publicly available. Moreover, they provide a wide coverage for large- scale mapping. Out of these, MSI was the most used, followed by HSI and SAR. Based on this review, we posit that the fusion of SAR and HSI datasets will benefit from detailed vegetation analysis, water quality from rich spectral information, and all-weather imaging. However, first, misalignment between varying datasets must be achieved for an accurate classification. In conclusion, this current review spearheads state-of-the-art models for handling com- plex datasets and their avenues of improvement. Finally, our analysis drives the direction of future work and contributes to effective and strategic wetland classification research. Author contributions D. E: Conceptualisation, M. A, A. Z, and Y. JSON: Name: mamba_ttt_noisy_wetland Title: Test-time training with a mamba-based spectral-spatial transformer and hybrid noise-robust loss for cross-scene hyperspectral wetland classification Short Hypothesis: Applying test-time training using a mamba-based spectral-spatial transformer model together with a hybrid focal-KL consistency loss on unlabeled target-domain hyperspectral wetland imagery will increase mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) on unseen target scenes by at least 5 percentage points relative to the identical model evaluated without test-time training. Related Work: Prior work has applied CNNs and U-Net variants to static wetland segmentation and 3D/2D CNNs or hybrid CNN-transformer architectures to exploit spectral-spatial cues; transformers improved long-range spectral modeling on hyperspectral imagery but incur high compute costs. Data-fusion methods (HSI+LiDAR, MSI+SAR) and adversarial domain-adaptation networks address modality complementarity and cross-scene shifts but typically require large, well-annotated source domains. Generative models (GANs, diffusion) have been used to augment scarce labels but suffer from mode collapse or unrealistic samples. Few-shot and weak supervision approaches are underexplored in wetland HSI. Test-time training and self-supervised pretext tasks have improved robustness in other vision domains, but their application to hyperspectral cross-scene wetland classification and to noisy labels remains limited. Existing limitations include sensitivity to label noise, insufficient single-source generalisation, high compute for transformer variants, and lack of evaluations that combine test-time adaptation with noise-robust objectives on real wetland HSI. Abstract: We address cross-scene hyperspectral wetland classification under limited and noisy labels by combining a computationally efficient spectral-spatial mamba transformer with test-time training and a hybrid noise-robust loss. The proposed pipeline trains a mamba-based encoder on source wetland scenes with an auxiliary self-supervised spectral masking task and a hybrid classification objective that blends focal loss for class imbalance and a KL-based consistency term to tolerate label noise. At inference, an unsupervised test-time training stage refines encoder parameters on each unlabeled target scene using the same auxiliary task and the consistency term, enabling on-the-fly adaptation to spectral shift. The main contribution is the integration of mamba's linear-complexity sequence modeling with a test-time adaptation protocol and noise-aware loss to improve segmentation robustness across unseen wetland domains. Expected outcomes are statistically significant gains in mIoU and per-class F1 on unseen wetland scenes, reduced degradation under injected label noise, and lower compute than full-scale transformer baselines, enabling more reliable transfer for operational wetland mapping. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Yellow River Delta (YRD) hyperspectral wetland dataset (ZY-1 / GF-type HSI) as primary source; (2) Huanghekou (HHK) hyperspectral wetland dataset as unseen target; (3) Yancheng (YC) HSI / sentinel-sourced benchmark dataset; (4) optional multimodal test set: Sentinel-2 MSI + Sentinel-1 SAR co-registered pairs for an MSI+SAR fusion ablation. Preprocessing: apply geometric co-registration, atmospheric correction to surface reflectance, per-band standardisation; extract fixed-size spectral-spatial patches (e.g., 11x11 spatial, full-spectrum tokens) for model input. Baselines: (A) mamba spectral-spatial transformer without TTT (same architecture, no adaptation); (B) Swin-transformer variant with and without TTT; (C) 3D-CNN (state-of-the-art HSI CNN); (D) U-Net segmentation; (E) adversarial domain-adaptation network trained on source(s). Ablations: (1) loss ablation: cross-entropy, focal, CE+KL, focal+KL (proposed); (2) auxiliary pretext ablation for TTT: spectral masking reconstruction vs. contrastive spectral prediction; (3) TTT ablation: 0, 10, 50, 200 adaptation gradient steps per test scene; (4) fusion ablation: HSI-only vs. HSI+LiDAR or MSI+SAR. Training/validation protocol: train on combined source scenes (YRD+YC) with 5 random seeds; validate on held-out source tiles. Cross-scene evaluation: test on fully unseen HHK tiles. Label-noise experiments: inject symmetric label flip at 0%, 10%, 20%, 40% in source training labels and measure robustness. Few-shot experiments: limit source labels to K={1,5,10} shots per class for secondary evaluation. Hyperparameters: optimizer AdamW, base learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 1e-4, batch size 64 (patches), training epochs 200; TTT adaptation uses lr 1e-5 for adaptation steps on each test tile. Hardware: experiments run on 2x NVIDIA A100 GPUs with mixed precision. Metrics: primary metric mean IoU (mIoU); secondary metrics overall accuracy (OA), mean F1 and per-class F1, Cohen's kappa, and robustness gap defined as delta mIoU between clean and noisy-label regimes. Statistical protocol: report mean ± std over 5 seeds; significance test: paired t-test comparing proposed method vs best baseline (alpha=0.05). Expected comparisons: proposed (mamba+TTT+focal+KL) vs mamba without TTT, vs Swin+TTT, vs adversarial DA, and loss ablation results. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: test-time training may overfit to short-lived or anomalous target-scene patterns, producing degraded segmentation for heterogeneous tiles; auxiliary pretext task may not correlate with downstream segmentation and thus provide weak adaptation signals. Data and evaluation biases: available wetland HSI datasets are region-specific and limited in diversity, producing evaluation bias and limited external validity; label noise injection in experiments may not fully emulate real-world annotation errors (systematic mislabeling). Scalability and compute: although mamba reduces sequence complexity, per-scene TTT adaptation increases inference time and GPU memory usage, limiting applicability to large-area operational mapping. Fusion and registration limits: multimodal fusion requires accurate co-registration; misalignment between HSI and LiDAR/SAR can introduce artifacts that reduce performance. Generalisation limits: adaptation on an unlabeled target improves local performance but cannot guarantee robustness to extreme spectral shifts or new classes not present in source training; the method assumes target scenes contain the same label set as the source. Experimental reproducibility: exact sensor characteristics and preprocessing pipelines vary across datasets, which may hinder replication without access to the same raw acquisitions.
